title: model-loading-weight-management-specs
content:
Purpose
This design doc defines model loading and weight management strategies for the Redwood serving runtime. It covers lazy loading, memory-mapped weights (mmap), safetensors support, hot-swap semantics, eviction policies, interactions with kernel selection and scheduling, and KV cache implications. The goal is a pragmatic, production-ready design that minimizes cold-start latency, reduces memory footprint across concurrent models, and enables safe live updates.

Context and motivation
- We run many models (open and tuned variants) across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Constrained GPU/CPU memory and varying model sizes (7B->70B) require flexible weight residency strategies.
- Operators want: fast cold starts, predictable memory usage, safe live rollouts (hot-swap), and clear failure modes.
- Implementation must integrate with the serving runtime kernel selection and the scheduler (batching threads, inference workers) and must not regress tail latency or stability.

Non-goals
- This doc does not specify low-level kernel code changes (those are in kernel RFCs).
- We do not mandate a single on-disk weight format for model authors beyond supporting safetensors and PyTorch state_dict payloads.

Requirements
- R1: Support both eager and lazy weight load for model parts (layers, attention blocks, embeddings).
- R2: Support memory-mapped weight access (mmap) for read-only weights to reduce RAM usage and facilitate fast process startup.
- R3: Support safetensors on-disk for secure, fast deserialization.
- R4: Provide API/CLI for hot-swapping model artifacts with safe validation and rollback.
- R5: Provide eviction strategy to free GPU/CPU memory when reservoir is full while minimizing perf impact.
- R6: Ensure compatibility with quantized weights (int8/4bit) and fused-kernel variants.
- R7: Expose observability (load time, mmap faults, bytes resident, eviction counts).

Key concepts and definitions
- Weight shard: contiguous tensor or group of tensors that can be loaded/mapped independently (e.g., a transformer block weightset).
- Residency: where the weight bytes currently live: disk-only, host-RAM, GPU-memory, or mmaped (host-addressable via page faults).
- Lazy load: defer materializing weight bytes into the target resident memory until first use.
- Hot-swap: replacing a model artifact (weights + config) in a running process/worker without client-visible errors; includes validation and rollback paths.
- Backing store: the on-disk representation (safetensors or state_dict) used as authoritative artifact.

Design overview
We propose a layered approach:
1) artifact ingestion & layout
2) memory-mapped read-only path for disk-backed weights
3) lazy load into target residency on first access or based on heuristics
4) weight promotion/ejection policy (host<->GPU) with LRU + cost heuristics
5) hot-swap protocol for live updates with safety checks

1) Artifact ingestion & layout
- Artifacts are stored as: 
  - preferred: safetensors (.safetensors) with a lightweight index mapping tensor name -> offset,length,dtype,shape
  - fallback: PyTorch zip state_dict (.pt/.pth) for models not produced with safetensors
- During ingestion (push to model store) we run a normalization step: validate tensor shapes/dtypes, compute per-tensor checksums (sha256), produce a metadata manifest (model.manifest.json) with the shard layout. The manifest is small and therefore loaded eagerly.
- We also produce optional quantized variants and kernel-compatible layout hints: contiguous storage, packing for fused kernels, and preferred memory order.

2) Memory-mapped read-only path (mmap)
Motivation: mmap reduces process startup time and avoids duplicating host RAM copies across processes. Implementation:
- For safetensors: we write tensors as packed contiguous byte ranges and record offsets. Workers open the file read-only and create mmap mappings for the whole file (or the subset needed) with MAP_SHARED.
- On platforms where mmap to GPU is supported (future), we can explore mapping through CUDA unified memory or direct GPU reads; initially GPU transfer remains explicit (cudaMemcpy) from page faulted host RAM.
- We treat mmap as read-only backing: when a weight is required in GPU memory it is forwarded from the mmapped region (which will trigger OS page-ins as needed).
- Observability: count and surface major page faults per model load, bytes populated.
Pros/Cons:
- + Fast process start, low host-RAM footprint in ideal OS-managed case.
- - Page-fault storms on first use can cause tail latency spikes; we mitigate with prefetching heuristics (see lazy load heuristics).

3) Lazy load heuristics and policies
Approaches:
- On-demand: load tensor bytes to GPU only when the kernel requests them. Good for large models where not all weights are used (e.g., Mixture-of-Experts shards).
- Prefetch-on-warmup: when a model is cold-loaded for a route, spawn a background warm-up thread that touches high-priority tensors in a prioritized order (embeddings, first N transformer layers, attention keys/values) to reduce first-request latency.
- Size/usage-based thresholds: for models > X GB or when concurrent model count > Y, default to mmap+on-demand. For smaller models (< 4GB), eager pre-load to GPU may be default.
- Kernel-driven hints: the kernel selection layer can annotate tensor access patterns (seqlen, layer order) so loader can prefetch specific shards.
- Batch-access hints: when scheduler forms a batch that will iterate through layers deterministically, we can prefetch upcoming layers during decoding.

Implementation details:
- WeightKey: unique id = model_version + tensor_name + checksum
- Loader maintains a per-worker residency table: entry = {WeightKey, residency_state, last_access_ts, pinned_flag, resident_bytes}
- API: Loader::resolve(tensor_name) -> ResidencyHandle
  - If on GPU: return pointer
  - If mmaped only: initiate async transfer to GPU, optionally block if caller requires immediate access
  - If not present on disk: error (invalid model)
- Async transfers use a prioritized transfer queue; transfers are cancellable if preemption needed for higher-priority requests.

4) Promotion/ejection policy (host<->GPU memory)
Goals: keep hottest tensors on GPU to minimize transfer latency, but respect GPU memory budgets.
Policy components:
- Soft quota per-worker and global reservation per-model: workers attempt to keep a model-reservation but can be preempted.
- Scoring: score = alpha * recency_score + beta * frequency_score + gamma * gpu_transfer_cost_estimate - delta * size_penalty
- Eviction: choose lowest score non-pinned shards and evict to host (or drop if host also constrained). Eviction triggers async cudaFree and metadata update.
- Pinned weights: certain tensors (embedding table, output head) can be pinned to GPU based on model config or runtime policy.
- Batch awareness: scheduler informs loader of imminent layer sequence so loader can prefetch and avoid eviction of next-step weights.

5) Hot-swap protocol
We need an atomic and observable hot-swap flow for model version rollouts. Requirements: zero or bounded client-visible errors, ability to rollback.
Protocol outline:
- Upload new artifact to model store and produce new manifest + checksums.
- Controller triggers a staged rollout: for each worker process:
  1. Acquire model-swap lock for the worker.
  2. Validate: check manifest, sample tensor checksums against store, and optionally run a short deterministic inference test (smoke test) on a pinned warmup prompt.
  3. Load new manifest; perform lazy mmap open of new backing file(s).
  4. Warm-up phase (optional): prefetch pinned tensors or first-N layers based on policy.
  5. Switch route handler pointers atomically so new requests use new model_version. Requests in-flight continue referencing the old ResidencyHandles.
  6. Decommission old weights: decrement refcounts; start eviction timer. If old model has zero active in-flight requests and no pinned weights, free resources.
- Rollback: controller can reverse pointer switch; workers will bring old residency back to active if needed. Must maintain both old and new mmaps during transition window.
Safety and failure modes:
- If smoke test fails, abort switch and keep serving old model. Surface metrics and failure reason.
- If new model is too large to fit even after eviction, fail the rollout for that worker and mark as "insufficient capacity". Controller can route to fallback model variant.

KV cache interactions
- KV cache is independent per-inference session and is stored in GPU memory (or CPU for large/archival sessions).
- Weight management must prioritize weights over KV cache: while weights are read-only shared across sessions, KV cache is per-session and has weaker locality between sessions.
- When memory pressure forces eviction, prefer evicting KV cache entries of least-recent sessions before evicting model weights, unless eviction of weights is unavoidable.
- Eviction policy must communicate with the scheduler to consider session priorities (e.g., paid-tier sessions pinned longer).

Quantization and kernel compatibility
- Loader will support multiple on-disk representations: fp32, fp16, int8/int4 (quantized), and packed formats for fused kernels.
- Manifest includes weight_variant entries mapping logical tensor -> file variant (e.g., layer1.wght.fp16.safetensors, layer1.wght.int8.packed)
- During resolve(), the loader picks the variant that balances quality and cost per routing policy. A fallback pipeline will convert between variants if needed (e.g., dequantize) but we prefer pre-generated variants to avoid runtime cost.

Observability and metrics
Expose per-model and per-worker metrics:
- model_load_time_seconds (cold load)
- mmap_page_faults_total
- bytes_mapped_host
- bytes_resident_gpu
- weight_evictions_total
- hot_swap_attempts_total, hot_swap_failures_total
- transfer_queue_latency_seconds (percentiles)
- residency_entries_count
Logs and traces:
- Detailed timeline for hot swap events, eviction decisions, and transfer prefetch actions.

Operational runbook (short)
- Cold start high latency: check mmap_page_faults and transfer queue backlog. Consider adjusting prefetch windows or increasing eager load for that model.
- Hot-swap smoke test failures: inspect model.manifest checksums, run local unit inference, ensure artifact ingestion completed successfully.
- Memory pressure: identify top resident tensors by bytes_resident_gpu and eviction counts; consider increasing global GPU pool or tuning per-model reservations.

Open design questions / TODOs
- Q1: Should we allow writable mmaps for models that require on-disk persistent KV cache in private deployments? (security and corruption risk).
- Q2: Investigate OS-specific optimizations for page fault batching or madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) for Linux. Implement tuning knobs.
- Q3: Explore direct GPU-backed page mappings (ROCm/CUDA) for zero-copy in future hardware.
- Q4: Define a standard layout for safetensors manifest that supports sharded cross-file references.
- Q5: Define heuristics to auto-generate pinned tensor lists based on early traffic.

Implementation plan & milestones (quarterly)
- Sprint 1 (4 weeks): safetensors ingestion + manifest generation; mmapping read-only safetensors in worker; simple resolve() that blocks and copies to GPU synchronously.
- Sprint 2 (6 weeks): async transfer queue, residency table, basic eviction (LRU), metrics for mmap faults and transfers.
- Sprint 3 (6 weeks): hot-swap control flow, smoke test harness, staged rollout orchestration in controller.
- Sprint 4 (8 weeks): kernel-driven prefetch hints, scheduler integration, quantized variant selection, and production rollout for selected models.

Backwards compatibility & migration notes
- Existing .pt artifacts remain supported but should be re-ingested to safetensors to gain mmap benefits. During migration we will accept both and convert lazily at ingestion time.

Security considerations
- Validate checksums and signatures of model artifacts before mapping or loading.
- Ensure mmap files have correct ownership/permissions in multi-tenant environments; recommend copy-on-read into private workspace if tenant isolation required.

Appendix: example pseudocode (simplified)
- resolve(tensor):
  entry = residency_table.lookup(tensor)
  if entry.residency == GPU: return entry.gpu_ptr
  if entry.residency == MMAP or entry.residency == DISK:
    enqueue_transfer(tensor, priority=compute_priority())
    if caller.blocking: wait_for_transfer_completion()
    return entry.gpu_ptr_after_transfer
  error

- evacuation loop:
  while gpu_usage > target_budget:
    candidate = pick_lowest_score_nonpinned()
    if candidate == null: break
    evict_to_host(candidate)

Notes / author comments
- This is intentionally conservative: favor safety and observability over aggressive prefetching that could cause unpredictable tail spikes.
- We must prototype mmap + async transfer and measure page-fault patterns on typical production workloads (chat decoding, few-shot prompts with long context).

Contact and next steps
- Owner: Sofia Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Please review and add comments inline in the Drive doc. After design sign-off, we will open implementation PRs under the serving-runtime repo and schedule a cross-team sync with console, scheduler, and ops.
